clues: A paired trabeculated venous channel situated on either side of the sella turcica and body of the sphenoid bone.
Its lateral dural wall transmits cranial nerves III, IV, V1, and V2.
The internal carotid artery and abducens nerve (CN VI) pass directly through its lumen.
A short paired channel situated immediately posterior to the columns of the fornix.
It contains a portion of the choroid plexus extending from the roof of the midline ventricle.
It allows cerebrospinal fluid to drain from each lateral ventricle into the third ventricle.
The tapered inferior extremity of the spinal cord.
In a normal adult, it terminates at the level of the first or second lumbar vertebra.
The filum terminale extends downward from its apex while the cauda equina surrounds it.
A band of myelinated axons crossing the midline just ventral to the central canal of the spinal cord.
Second-order neurons carrying pain and temperature decussate through this structure.
It is selectively damaged early in cervical syringomyelia, causing cape-like sensory loss.
A rounded prominence on the dorsal floor of the fourth ventricle in the caudal pons.
It lies medial to the sulcus limitans.
It is formed by motor fibers of CN VII looping around the underlying abducens nucleus.
An elongated column of special visceral efferent motor neurons in the reticular formation of the medulla.
It innervates striated muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx via CN IX, X, and cranial XI.
Lesions here in lateral medullary syndrome produce dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of the gag reflex.
A large, flask-shaped neuron arranged in a single middle layer of the cerebellar cortex.
It possesses an elaborate flat dendritic arborization that receives climbing and parallel fibers.
Its inhibitory GABAergic axon forms the sole output of the cerebellar cortex.
A six-layered thalamic relay structure located on the posterior underside of the pulvinar.
It receives retinotopic axons traveling in the optic tract.
It projects via the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
A biconvex lens-shaped diencephalic nucleus situated ventral to the thalamus and dorsal to the substantia nigra.
It provides excitatory glutamatergic drive to the internal segment of the globus pallidus.
A vascular lesion here produces contralateral violent flinging movements known as hemiballismus.
Small deep penetrating vessels arising primarily from the horizontal M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery.
They enter the brain through the anterior perforated substance.
They supply the internal capsule and basal ganglia and are the most common site of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage.
A curved bidirectional bundle of white matter association fibers arching around the posterior Sylvian fissure.
It links the posterior superior temporal gyrus with the inferior frontal gyrus.
Damage to this tract disrupts repetition of spoken words, causing conduction aphasia.
A C-shaped bundle of projection and commissural fibers curving beneath the corpus callosum.
It arises from the fimbria of the hippocampus and arches forward over the thalamus.
Its anterior columns descend behind the anterior commissure to end in the mammillary bodies.

terms.sub: Cerebral Blood Supply and Circle of Willis
clues: The largest segmental medullary feeder reinforcing the anterior spinal artery in the lower thoracic or upper lumbar region.
It most commonly arises on the left side between T8 and L2.
Iatrogenic injury during abdominal aortic aneurysm repair causes anterior spinal cord infarction and paraplegia.
A downward displacement of the medial temporal lobe across the free margin of the tentorium cerebelli.
It compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve, producing a fixed dilated pupil.
Further progression compresses the cerebral peduncle, leading to contralateral hemiparesis and coma.
